Tony generates the pairing code with `openclaw qr --limited` instead of the default admin handoff. `--voice-node` is not for a parent's phone: it drops the write scope, so typed chat (`chat.send`) and the Listen action (`tts.speak`) stop working, and whether Talk still runs is untested. Native Talk is a loop: Apple Speech recognition on the phone, Gateway chat on the chosen agent (tony-main or jordan-main), then `talk.speak` playback. `talk.speak` reads the Talk block, not the `tts` block: set `talk.provider` plus `talk.providers.<id>` to a speech provider (the local engine from VOX-04 can be named there); with no Talk provider the gateway call fails and the docs mention an iPhone system-voice fallback. Keys: `talk.agentId` (owner when the client sends no agent-prefixed session key), `talk.speechLocale`, `talk.silenceTimeoutMs`, `talk.interruptOnSpeech`. Entry points: the inline Talk control, the `Start Live Voice` App Shortcut, the Siri phrase, or the Action Button.

corrections.how: Pair by device type with `openclaw qr`. A parent's phone that also chats gets `--limited` (no operator.admin; still operator.write, operator.approvals and operator.talk.secrets). A talk-only client such as a room device gets `--voice-node` (node token plus only operator.read and operator.talk, so no chat.send and no tts.speak). Set `talk.agentId` explicitly, because a multi-agent gateway has no unambiguous Talk owner. Use `talk.realtime.brain: agent-consult` and keep the built-in spoken-confirmation gate. Leave `tts.modelOverrides.allowProvider` off (its default) so a reply directive cannot move speech to a cloud provider. Add a read-only device and scope listing to the operator's inspect script. For hard per-person enforcement the documented route is `gateway.roles` (named operator roles that restrict agents and scopes for verified identities).
caveats: operator.read is documented as not being a per-person privacy boundary: a talk-only device can still read gateway status and session data across agents.
Talk clients choose the agent (the Watch literally asks which agent), so 'Jordan's device only reaches jordan-main' is not enforced without gateway roles.
There is no speaker identification anywhere in the stack. Whoever is near the microphone is the user; the FaceTime doc says the same about its own calls.
With roles configured, plain device or bootstrap tokens are rejected for operator connections, so roles change how every app signs in. That is a bigger project than voice.

Scopes limit which gateway methods a device may call, not which agent it reaches. A device names the session key for its own Talk sessions, and the installed gateway also accepts a node-level voice-transcript event that starts an agent run on whatever session key the device supplies (the main session if none). Pinning a device to one agent needs `gateway.roles` or stays a client-side convention.

Tightening a phone's scope has a price: without operator.admin the app's Settings pages (including this device's Talk and Voice Wake switches) do not open, and standalone Watch voice cannot be set up from that phone.

`talk.agentId` is one value for the whole gateway, so it cannot mean each parent's own agent. Whichever agent it names receives every Talk session that arrives without an agent-prefixed key, so it should be a memory-less one.
The default and the limited handoff both include operator.talk.secrets (read Talk configuration with secrets included).
unverified: Whether the iOS and Watch apps still connect once `gateway.roles` is configured.
Whether anything short of `gateway.roles` pins a device to one agent; the installed node-event code takes the session key from the device.
Whether the kill switch hooks in G005 fire for realtime Talk sessions.

corrections.how: Gateway `tts` block. Documented option A: Speech Swift's local server on loopback (`brew install speech`, `speech-server --port 8080`) with the `openai` speech provider pointed at the loopback base URL, `model` tts-1 (which selects Kokoro) and `responseFormat` wav. Option B: `tts-local-cli` running the `speech` or `say` command. Option C: a Piper voice through sherpa-onnx; the bundled sherpa-onnx-tts skill runs a local binary from a shell, which needs an exec tool no agent here has, so in practice point `tts-local-cli` at that binary. In every option set `tts.providers.microsoft.enabled: false`, so the default-on Microsoft online provider cannot serve as a fallback when the local engine fails. Per-agent control through `agents.entries.<id>.tts` (off for research and inbox). `tts.auto: inbound` gives a voice answer to a voice memo; `/tts latest` reads the previous reply. ffmpeg on the host for conversions.
corrections.safety: Speech synthesis is an output transformation on the gateway host and adds no new way for an agent to send data out. No text leaves the Mac for TTS only when three things hold: the selected engine is loopback or CLI, the Microsoft online provider is disabled so it cannot act as a fallback, and long-reply summaries are off or use a local model (the summary step calls the chat model). That combination is what the kids' cloud-TTS rule requires. Keep provider switching by directive off (VOX-03).
caveats: iMessage is not a voice-note channel: the reply is an audio file attachment, not a voice bubble. The voice-bubble option (`asVoice` on upload-file) belongs to the Private API action set, which needs SIP off.
Local engines emit WAV, so a few minutes of speech is several megabytes.
Long replies are summarized by the chat model before synthesis (a cloud call) or truncated.
Two tempting shortcuts are cloud services and must stay off for kids' content: the no-key Microsoft provider (Edge online TTS) and the bundled `sag` skill (ElevenLabs).
The built-in `tts` tool only speaks when asked, which is the right default: nobody wants every text reply doubled as audio.
The loopback route needs Speech Swift v0.0.23 or later. It is a 0.0.x project, so pin the version and expect rough edges; the server also needs its own launchd job to stay up.
None of `speech`, `speech-server` or `ffmpeg` is installed on this Mac today.
iMessage outbound media is capped by `channels.imessage.mediaMaxMb` (default 16 MB), which bounds the length of a WAV reply.
unverified: Kokoro or Piper voice quality and speed on this Mac.
Whether pointing `tts.providers.openai` at loopback has any side effect on the earlier decision not to add a catalog openai model provider (it is a different config block).
Whether scheduled announce deliveries (briefs) pass through Auto-TTS or only interactive replies do.

Whether a failed local synthesis actually falls through to the Microsoft online provider when only one provider block is written. The docs say other configured providers are fallbacks and that Microsoft is enabled by default; this was not tested.

corrections.how: App Store OpenClaw app on the spare phone, signed in with a household Apple Account rather than a parent's. Tailscale on the phone. Pair with `openclaw qr --voice-node` so the device holds only a node token plus operator.read and operator.talk. Guided Access pins the phone to the one app. The device's Voice Wake, Talk, background-listening, speakerphone and keep-awake switches sit on Settings pages that open only on an operator.admin connection, which a voice-node pairing does not have: either set them once under a temporary full-access pairing and then re-pair as a voice node (untested whether they persist), or treat the terminal as tap-to-talk only from the inline Talk control in Chat. Point `talk.agentId` (or the app's agent picker) at a new stateless kitchen agent with a short allowlist (weather, list add, calendar read), never at tony-main or jordan-main; this is a client-side choice, not something the pairing enforces.

local model before kids may use it
caveats: iOS voice features are best-effort unless the app stays in the foreground, hence Guided Access plus keep-awake. Months of always-on use on a charger is untested.

Kids will talk to it. Every agent today is cloud-backed, so under the family's own rule this terminal is for parents only until a local model exists. Guided Access controls taps, not voices.

A talk-only device can still read gateway status (operator.read).

If the only path that works is realtime Talk, the terminal inherits VOX-02: room audio goes to OpenAI for the length of each session.

corrections.how: Buy the device. Run Home Assistant OS in a VM on the Mac (documented minimum 2 GB RAM and 2 vCPUs; a VirtualBox image for Apple Silicon, or UTM). Add Whisper or Speech-to-Phrase for speech-to-text and Piper for speech through the Wyoming integration for a fully local pipeline. Then a conversation agent must forward the text to a stateless OpenClaw agent, and that hop is the unsolved part: Home Assistant's official OpenAI integration only talks to OpenAI's own endpoint, and OpenClaw's OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint (off by default; the config repo's flat config has it enabled on this gateway) is documented as full operator access.
